Gluon. Gluons are massless gauge bosons that mediate the strong nuclear force by coupling to color charge. Eight gluons exist—each carrying a color-anticolor pair, such as red-antiblue—and bind quarks within hadrons. Unlike photons, gluons interact with themselves, creating self-coupling phenomena that generate most of the mass in ordinary matter.

Gluons are spin-one gauge bosons that are massless and confined like quarks. There are eight types, representing three colors times three anticolors, minus one singlet, technically forming an SU(three) octet. Each gluon carries both color charge and anticolor charge. They couple with strength determined by the strong coupling constant, approximately zero point one two at typical scales. A unique feature sets gluons apart from other force carriers: gluons can emit or absorb other gluons. This self-interaction is absent in electromagnetism and is central to quantum chromodynamics. Through gluon self-interaction, the strong coupling exhibits running behavior—it weakens at high energy and strengthens at low energy. This beta function property, called asymptotic freedom, governs all hadron phenomenology.

Gluons are responsible for roughly ninety-nine percent of the proton's mass through binding energy, despite quarks contributing only about one percent. The self-coupling of gluons creates non-abelian dynamics unique to quantum chromodynamics. This nonlinearity explains color confinement—why quarks cannot escape hadrons—and generates the rich spectrum of resonances observed in hadron collisions.
